# Colour

Source: *The UI/UX Playbook* (uxpeak). Each entry separates **what the PDF states** from **our interpretation of its images**. Text explanations are complete without the images. Back to the [index](../index.md).

<a id="col-01"></a>
## COL-01 - Use the primary colour sparingly

If everything is in the primary colour, nothing stands out; reserve it mainly for key interactive elements so it works as a cue for where to click.

- **Source:** PDF 66 (printed 65), 67 (printed 66)
- **Applies when:** Applying brand/primary colour across a screen.

**What the PDF states** (paraphrased):
- Less is often more: overusing primary colours overwhelms and looks unbalanced and messy.
- When everything is highlighted, nothing stands out and colour stops guiding interactivity.
- Use the primary colour thoughtfully, mostly for clickable elements such as buttons and links; too many colours have the same cluttering effect.

**Mistake:** Brand colour on icons, titles, section headers, every button and nav icons.  
**Effect:** No focal point; colour loses meaning.

**Correction:** Neutral base with the primary colour on a few key interactive elements.  
**Why it works:** Scarcity gives the colour signalling power.

**Observable checks:**
- Estimate the share of elements using the primary colour; is it on non-interactive text such as headings?
- Do more than one or two element types per view carry the primary colour?

**Exceptions / limits supported by the source:**
- None stated by the source.

**Interpretation (ours, not stated by the PDF):**
- In the corrected banking app even Send/Request become grey neutral buttons; 'mostly clickable elements' is guidance, not a requirement to colour every clickable element.

**Related:** [BAL-02](10-balance.md#bal-02), [VH-01](02-visual-hierarchy.md#vh-01), [CNS-02](11-consistency.md#cns-02)

<a id="col-02"></a>
## COL-02 - Prefer neutral backgrounds; vibrant only for special areas

Neutral backgrounds (greys, beige, soft whites) let content and accents pop; vibrant full backgrounds clash and reduce readability. Dark backgrounds can work well.

- **Source:** PDF 67 (printed 66), 68 (printed 67), 69 (printed 68)
- **Applies when:** Choosing page and app background colours.

**What the PDF states** (paraphrased):
- A neutral background is often the way to go: a clean canvas that lets content and primary colours pop.
- A vibrant saturated background can seem dynamic but is less clear, overwhelming, clashes with text and UI and reduces readability.
- Coloured backgrounds can work for splash screens, headers and specialised sections.
- Dark backgrounds are great too: contrast makes text pop, and they are easier on the eyes in low light (less glare and eye strain).

**Mistake:** A whole app screen on a saturated purple background.  
**Effect:** Overwhelming; text and UI clash with the background.

**Correction:** White/neutral or dark neutral background, with colour reserved for accents.  
**Why it works:** Neutral surfaces minimise distraction and guide attention.

**Observable checks:**
- Is a high-saturation colour used as the main background for content-heavy screens (not just splash/header areas)?

**Exceptions / limits supported by the source:**
- Coloured backgrounds are acceptable for splash screens, headers and specialised sections.
- Dark (near-black, desaturated) backgrounds are acceptable and often good.

**Source issues / ambiguity:**
- The portfolio example labels two segments 'Cash' (25% and 60%); a source labelling slip unrelated to the lesson.

**Related:** [COL-01](14-color.md#col-01), [COL-03](14-color.md#col-03)

<a id="col-03"></a>
## COL-03 - Offer dark mode where it serves users and brand

Many users expect a choice between light and dark; the decision should consider UX and fit the brand.

- **Source:** PDF 70 (printed 69)
- **Applies when:** Products deciding on theme support.

**What the PDF states** (paraphrased):
- For many users dark mode is a must-have; offering light and dark is inclusive and versatile; the choice should consider UX and align with the brand.

**Mistake:** Not considering theme choice at all.  
**Effect:** Excludes users who prefer dark interfaces.

**Correction:** Evaluate and, where appropriate, offer both themes.  
**Why it works:** Inclusivity and comfort.

**Observable checks:**
- Does the product's audience/context justify a dark theme option?

**Exceptions / limits supported by the source:**
- None stated by the source.

**Source issues / ambiguity:**
- Text-only recommendation; no visual comparison.

**Related:** [COL-02](14-color.md#col-02)

*No visual example: the PDF presents this point in text only.*

<a id="col-04"></a>
## COL-04 - Don't rely on colour alone to communicate state

Pair status colours with icons, text labels or patterns, because of colour-vision deficiencies and varying lighting.

- **Source:** PDF 70 (printed 69)
- **Applies when:** Errors, warnings, success states, charts, status indicators.

**What the PDF states** (paraphrased):
- Relying solely on colour for states (error, success, warning) is a common pitfall; combine colour with icons, text labels or patterns.

**Mistake:** An invalid input marked only by a red border.  
**Effect:** Users with colour-vision deficiency, or in poor lighting, miss the error and its cause.

**Correction:** Red border plus an error icon plus a message explaining the fix (e.g. 'Enter amount bigger than $1').  
**Why it works:** Redundant cues reach everyone.

**Observable checks:**
- For every state shown with colour, is there also an icon or text?
- Do error states explain what to do?

**Exceptions / limits supported by the source:**
- None stated by the source.

**Related:** [COL-05](14-color.md#col-05), [STA-02](19-content-and-states.md#sta-02), [CON-01](06-contrast.md#con-01)

<a id="col-05"></a>
## COL-05 - Follow colour conventions for system status

Red means error/stop and green means success/go; don't use yellow for errors or pink for success, even if on-brand. Adjust tones, not meanings.

- **Source:** PDF 71 (printed 70)
- **Applies when:** Validation, alerts, toasts, status badges.

**What the PDF states** (paraphrased):
- Stick to widely accepted conventions: don't use yellow for errors or pink for success even if it matches the brand.
- Conventions based on years of use: red = stop/error, green = go/success; breaking them confuses and slows users.
- To fit a brand, adjust the tones of the conventional colours so they harmonise.

**Mistake:** Amber error state; pink success state.  
**Effect:** Users misread the state.

**Correction:** Red for errors, green for success, tuned in tone to the palette.  
**Why it works:** Leverages learned associations.

**Observable checks:**
- Map each status to its colour: is error red-family and success green-family?

**Exceptions / limits supported by the source:**
- None stated by the source.

**Related:** [COL-04](14-color.md#col-04), [DLG-01](18-dialogs.md#dlg-01)
